question: Assume today is 2026-08-23. You know nothing published after this date. Estimate the number of live births in South Korea in July 2026, as it will be first reported in the national statistics agency's monthly Population Trends release.

target.what: Number of live births occurring in South Korea during July 2026, as first reported in the national statistics agency's monthly Population Trends release
target.cadence: Monthly, typically released around the last week of the second following month (e.g., July data released late September 2026)
target.caveats: The target period is completed relative to the 2026-08-23 cutoff, but the official July 2026 figure is not yet published. The first report may be provisional and subject to revision. Live births are counted by date of occurrence, not registration date; late registration can cause small revisions. Th

candidates.hypothesis: July 2026 births can be estimated by applying recent year-over-year growth rates or seasonal factors to the same month in prior years. The most recent published months (e.g., May or June 2026) provide the latest level and trend, while July values from 2023–2025 provide the seasonal baseline.
candidates.data_to_find: Monthly live birth counts for South Korea from January 2023 through the latest available month before 2026-08-23 (likely May or June 2026), including July 2023, July 2024, and July 2025. Also useful: the year-over-year percent change for each month in 2025 and 2026 year-to-date.
search_hints: South Korea monthly birth statistics July 2025

candidates.perspective: Population registration and resident registration data
candidates.hypothesis: Monthly birth counts from KOSTAT are closely correlated with birth registrations in the resident registration system, though with a lag. If July 2026 registration data are available (e.g., from Ministry of Interior and Safety), they can serve as a leading indicator or cross-check for the KOSTAT figure.
candidates.data_to_find: Monthly number of birth registrations in South Korea's resident registration system for July 2026 (or the most recent months), and the historical relationship between registration counts and KOSTAT live birth counts (e.g., average ratio or lag).
search_hints: South Korea birth registration statistics July 2026

candidates.perspective: Hospital and health insurance claims for deliveries
candidates.hypothesis: The number of live births is strongly related to the number of delivery-related hospital admissions or health insurance claims for childbirth. National Health Insurance Service (NHIS) data on delivery claims can provide an independent estimate, adjusted for multiple births and coverage.
candidates.data_to_find: Monthly counts of health insurance claims for delivery (normal and cesarean) in South Korea for recent months, including July 2026 if available, and the historical ratio of live births to delivery claims.
search_hints: NHIS delivery claims South Korea monthly

candidates.hypothesis: Births can be estimated from the capacity and utilization of obstetric wards: number of obstetric beds, average length of stay, and occupancy rates. This route requires assumptions about the share of births in hospitals versus other settings, but can provide a lower-bound check.
candidates.data_to_find: Number of obstetric beds and average occupancy rate in South Korean hospitals for 2025–2026, average length of stay for delivery, and the share of births occurring in medical facilities.

candidates.hypothesis: Recent policy changes (e.g., parental benefits, housing support) or calendar effects (e.g., number of weekends, holidays) may have influenced births in July 2026. Quantifying these effects can adjust a baseline estimate.
candidates.data_to_find: Any major pronatalist policy announcements or changes in 2025–2026, their expected impact on births, and the number of weekend days and public holidays in July 2026 compared to prior years.

candidates.hypothesis: Statistics Korea or other institutions may publish monthly or quarterly birth projections that include July 2026. These can serve as a direct estimate or a benchmark.
candidates.data_to_find: Any published forecasts or projections of monthly live births for South Korea in 2026, especially for July, from KOSTAT, Bank of Korea, or research institutes.

candidates.hypothesis: The monthly birth series exhibits seasonality (e.g., higher births in certain months) and a long-term downward trend. A seasonal index and trend can be estimated from historical data to project July 2026 from a recent 12-month total or year-to-date total.
candidates.data_to_find: Monthly live birth counts for South Korea for at least 5 years (2021–2025) to estimate seasonal factors, and the year-to-date total for 2026 (January–June) to anchor the level.

candidates.hypothesis: Births in July 2026 are largely determined by conceptions around October 2025, which may correlate with marriage counts and fertility intentions. Marriage data from late 2025 and early 2026 can provide a leading indicator.
candidates.data_to_find: Monthly marriage counts in South Korea for 2025 and early 2026, and any survey data on fertility intentions or birth plans from late 2025.

assessment.note: Both are KOSTAT-derived monthly marriage growth rates for adjacent months (Oct and Nov 2025) from the same underlying registration series; they jointly indicate a modest but positive marriage uptick in late 2025, which is the conception-relevant window for July 2026 births. They are not independent of each other.

Seoul, Incheon and Gyeonggi cumulative Jan-Nov 2025 live-birth growth rates (8.7%, 8.4%, 6.8%) are all positive and mutually consistent, pointing to a genuine 2025 national birth rebound concentrated in the capital region. Same source and same measurement basis, so they corroborate rather than independently confirm.

Seoul cumulative Jan-Nov 2025 marriage growth (+15.8%) is consistent in sign with the national monthly marriage increases in Oct-Nov 2025; both support the view that marriages were rising into the conception window for mid-2026 births.
Lower and upper bounds of the same 2025 TFR forecast (0.78-0.80); they are two endpoints of one forecast, not independent observations.

All describe the same 2021-to-2025 contraction of obstetric/newborn inpatient capacity (newborn nursery beds/rooms, delivery beds/rooms, rooming-in rooms). They share one source and one measurement basis and jointly show capacity shrinking faster than births, so capacity is a weak and biased proxy for birth volume.

Operating-room and emergency-room bed counts are general hospital capacity indicators, not obstetric-specific; they show overall hospital capacity roughly flat and therefore do not corroborate or contradict the obstetric-capacity contraction.

Redundant upper endpoint of the same 2025 TFR forecast as p5; keeping both would double-count one forecast.

a.role: placeholder for the observed July 2025 national live-birth level, which is not in the kept set; this method is not executable as written

b.role: July 2026 national live births relative to July 2025 national live births

methods.rationale: Intended route: take the observed July 2025 national live-birth level and multiply by the year-on-year change factor a1. This is the most direct credible route, but it cannot be executed because no kept point supplies the July 2025 national live-birth level; p8-p10 are growth rates, not levels, and p5-p6 are TFR forecasts. The method is listed to make the missing input explicit; it should be replaced once b2 supplies the level.

a.role: placeholder for a 2025 annual national live-birth total, which p5 does not supply (it is a TFR forecast, not a birth count); this method is not executable as written

b.role: share of annual live births occurring in July

methods.rationale: Intended route: multiply an annual national live-birth total by the July share a2 to obtain July 2026 births. This is a valid decomposition in principle, but no kept point provides the annual birth total; p5/p6 are fertility-rate forecasts and p8-p10 are regional growth rates. The method is listed to flag that the annual-total input is missing and must come from b2.

assumptions.name: July 2026 national live births relative to July 2025 national live births
assumptions.rationale: The kept evidence points to a 2025 birth rebound (Seoul +8.7%, Incheon +8.4%, Gyeonggi +6.8% cumulative Jan-Nov 2025) and rising marriages in the conception window for July 2026 (national Oct +0.2%, Nov +2.7%; Seoul cumulative +15.8%). A modest positive year-on-year ratio for July 2026 is therefore the central case, but the national trend is weaker than the capital-region figures and the 2025 TFR forecast of 0.78-0.80 implies only a slow recovery, so the range spans a small decline to a solid increase.
assumptions.applies_when: Used only to scale an observed July 2025 national live-birth level to July 2026; it is a change factor, not a level of the target.
assumptions.falsified_by: A published July 2026 registration or KOSTAT figure showing a year-on-year change outside roughly -2% to +13%, or evidence that the 2025 marriage increase did not translate into 2026 conceptions.

assumptions.name: Share of annual live births occurring in July
assumptions.rationale: July is close to an average month in the Korean birth seasonal pattern, with a mild summer peak; a share near 1/12 with a small upward tilt is the central value, and the range covers the observed amplitude of Korean monthly birth seasonality.
assumptions.applies_when: Used to convert a 12-month or annual live-birth total into a July component; requires the total to cover a period containing July 2026.
assumptions.falsified_by: A published monthly seasonal index for Korean births showing July materially outside the 7.8-8.9% band.

assessment.note: Both are KOSTAT-derived marriage growth rates for adjacent months (Oct and Nov 2025) from the same source article; they jointly indicate a weak but positive marriage recovery in late 2025, which is the conception-relevant window for July 2026 births. They are not independent of each other.

Seoul, Incheon, and Gyeonggi cumulative live-birth growth rates for Jan–Nov 2025 are all positive and of similar magnitude (6.8–8.7%), from the same source. They corroborate a national-level birth increase in 2025 but are regional subsets, not independent national measurements.

Seoul cumulative marriage growth (15.8%) is much stronger than the national monthly marriage growth rates in p3/p4, consistent with a marriage-led birth rebound concentrated in the capital region; it supports the d5 conception-lag route but is a regional, not national, indicator.

Lower and upper bounds of the same 2025 TFR forecast (0.78–0.80); they are two endpoints of one forecast, not independent estimates. They provide context on the 2025 fertility level but do not directly give a July 2026 monthly birth count.

All are hospital-capacity counts from the same 2025-07-24 snapshot of one article. They consistently show declining obstetric/newborn capacity (delivery beds −16.5%, newborn nursery beds −9.1% from 2021 to 2025), which is a structural constraint on hospital deliveries but not a direct birth count. They share a single source and are not independent of one another.

decisions.reason: Annual TFR forecast lower bound; TFR is a period fertility intensity measure, not a monthly birth count, and the target is a July 2026 monthly level. It cannot be converted to the target without an assumed population and monthly seasonal share, which would be an invented coefficient. Retained only as context, not as a numerical input.
Annual TFR forecast upper bound; same ineligibility as p5. Redundant with p5 as the other endpoint of the same forecast.
Operating room beds are not delivery-specific capacity and have no defined conversion to births; irrelevant to the target.

Mother-and-baby rooming-in rooms are a post-delivery amenity count, not a delivery-capacity measure; no defensible conversion to births. Redundant with the broader capacity set.

a.role: July 2025 national monthly live-birth level in South Korea (base level, not the target)

b.role: July 2026 national live-birth change factor relative to July 2025

methods.rationale: July 2026 national live births = July 2025 national monthly live-birth level × change factor. The base level a3 is an assumption because no kept point supplies the KOSTAT July 2025 monthly count; the change factor a1 is supported by the late-2025 marriage uptick (p3, p4) and regional 2025 birth growth (p8–p10), tempered by the low TFR forecast (p5). Shared dependencies: both the base level and the factor rely on the same broad 2025 birth scale, so the interval is not fully independent. Failure mode: if the actual July 2025 level differs materially from a3, or if the 2025 rebound fades, the estimate shifts.

a.role: July 2025 national monthly live-birth level in South Korea (base level, not the target)

b.role: July 2026 national live-birth change factor relative to July 2025 (marriage-lag route)

methods.rationale: July 2026 national live births = July 2025 national monthly live-birth level × marriage-lag change factor. The base level a4 is an assumption for the missing KOSTAT July 2025 count; the factor a2 is anchored on Oct–Nov 2025 national marriage growth (p3, p4) and Seoul cumulative marriage growth (p11). Shared dependencies: a2 and a4 both rest on the same 2025 scale evidence, and the marriage-to-birth conversion is uncertain. Failure mode: a breakdown in the marriage-to-birth lag or a different July 2025 base would move the estimate.

assumptions.name: July 2026 national live-birth change factor relative to July 2025
assumptions.rationale: The conception window for July 2026 births is roughly October 2025. National marriage growth was weakly positive in Oct 2025 (p4, +0.2%) and Nov 2025 (p3, +2.7%), while regional cumulative live births in Jan–Nov 2025 rose 6.8–8.7% (p8, p9, p10), suggesting a modest national birth increase into 2026. The 2025 TFR forecast of 0.78–0.80 (p5) implies fertility remains near historic lows, and monthly birth growth is noisy. A central factor of 1.05 with a wide 0.95–1.16 range reflects a small positive carry-over from the 2025 marriage/birth uptick, tempered by continued low fertility and possible fading of the rebound.
assumptions.applies_when: A July 2025 national monthly live-birth level is available as the base, and the marriage-led birth increase observed in late 2025 continues at a similar or slightly weaker pace into July 2026.
assumptions.falsified_by: Evidence that national monthly live births in early 2026 turned negative year-on-year, or that the late-2025 marriage increase did not translate into a 2026 birth increase, would push the factor toward or below 1.0.

assumptions.name: July 2026 national live-birth change factor relative to July 2025 (marriage-lag route)
assumptions.rationale: Same conception-window logic as a1 but anchored more directly on the marriage series: Oct 2025 marriages +0.2% (p4) and Nov 2025 +2.7% (p3), with Seoul cumulative marriages +15.8% (p11). Because national monthly marriage growth is much weaker than the regional cumulative figure, the central factor is set slightly lower than a1. The wide range reflects the weak and noisy marriage signal and the uncertain marriage-to-birth conversion.
assumptions.applies_when: A July 2025 national monthly live-birth level is available and the marriage-to-birth lag of roughly 9 months holds for the Oct–Nov 2025 marriage cohort.

by_construction: Only URLs leave the searcher (code regex); extractor, judge and final prompts never contain search result titles, snippets or the searcher's text. This holds by construction and is not measured.
residual_risks: The searcher sees post-cutoff search results and chooses which URLs are fetched, so page selection can be conditioned on the answer; only the URLs leave the searcher, and in backtests every fetched page is a snapshot dated <= as_of.
Live pages are used only when as_of is today; in backtests every page is an archived snapshot dated <= as_of.
The leak sentinel only catches registered official values in common formats, not paraphrased or derived numbers.
The model's own training data (knowledge cutoff unpublished) can include history before as_of; it cannot include the target if the target was published after the model's release.
Wayback snapshots are captured by a third party; a snapshot date <= as_of proves the content existed by then.
Assumption values are proposed by the judge model from its own knowledge, which can include the target's history before as_of; code checks their form, not where the number came from.

ablation.rule: exclude points from own_history directions and points whose name contains a target entity anchor and whose name or unit shares a stem with the target unit (triangulate/agent/ablation.py)
residual_risks: Own values named by an alias or abbreviation, or with no entity in the point name, are not excluded.

The rule over-excludes on purpose: any point naming the target entity together with the target quantity (for example a survey of the target's visitors) is excluded, even when it is not a value of the target itself.
The model's own memory of the target's history is not removed: it can still shape the plan, the judge's choices and assumption values.
The searcher and the extractor still see pages that contain own values; only the judge's table is filtered.
